section.title: Unlawful Sexual Relations
section.sectionRationale: This is the first extended case law of the Holiness Code, addressing sexual ethics directly and grounding it not in the customs of Egypt or Canaan but in the identity of the LORD who redeemed Israel and now calls them to a different way of life.
section.thesis: God calls Israel to a sexual ethic entirely unlike Egypt's or Canaan's, prohibiting incest, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, same sex relations, and bestiality, because the land itself cannot bear such defilement and will vomit out those who practice it.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the call to walk in God's statutes rather than the customs of Egypt and Canaan; the list of forbidden family relations; a series of further prohibited unions and acts, including child sacrifice; and the closing warning that the land itself will not tolerate such defilement.

units.label: Not the customs of Egypt or Canaan
units.note: I am the LORD your God

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: I am the LORD your God.

You must not follow the practices of the land of Egypt, where you used to live, and you must not follow the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you. You must not walk in their customs.
You are to practice My judgments and keep My statutes by walking in them. I am the LORD your God.
Keep My statutes and My judgments, for the man who does these things will live by them. I am the LORD.

units.label: Family relations not to be uncovered

verses.text: None of you are to approach any close relative to have sexual relations. I am the LORD.
You must not expose the {{ervah|nakedness}} of your father by having sexual relations with your mother. She is your mother; you must not have sexual relations with her.
You must not have sexual relations with your father’s wife; it would dishonor your father.
You must not have sexual relations with your sister, either your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter, whether she was born in the same home or elsewhere.
You must not have sexual relations with your son’s daughter or your daughter’s daughter, for that would shame your family.
You must not have sexual relations with the daughter of your father’s wife, born to your father; she is your sister.
You must not have sexual relations with your father’s sister; she is your father’s close relative.
You must not have sexual relations with your mother’s sister, for she is your mother’s close relative.
You must not dishonor your father’s brother by approaching his wife to have sexual relations with her; she is your aunt.
You must not have sexual relations with your daughter-in-law. She is your son’s wife; you are not to have sexual relations with her.
You must not have sexual relations with your brother’s wife; that would shame your brother.

You must not have sexual relations with both a woman and her daughter. You are not to marry her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter and have sexual relations with her. They are close relatives; it is {{zimmah|depraved}}.
You must not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife and have sexual relations with her while your wife is still alive.

units.label: Further prohibitions
units.note: Molech, and every distortion of creation's order

verses.text: You must not approach a woman to have sexual relations with her during her menstrual period.
You must not lie carnally with your neighbor’s wife and thus defile yourself with her.
You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech, for you must not profane the name of your God. I am the LORD.
You must not lie with a man as with a woman; that is an {{toevah|abomination}}.
You must not lie carnally with any animal, thus defiling yourself with it; a woman must not stand before an animal to mate with it; that is a perversion.

units.label: The land itself will not bear it
units.note: a warning, not just a rule

verses.text: Do not defile yourselves by any of these practices, for by all these things the nations I am driving out before you have defiled themselves.
Even the land has become defiled, so I am punishing it for its sin, and the land will vomit out its inhabitants.
But you are to keep My statutes and ordinances, and you must not commit any of these abominations, neither your native-born nor the foreigner who lives among you.
For the men who were in the land before you committed all these abominations, and the land has become defiled.
So if you defile the land, it will vomit you out as it spewed out the nations before you.
Therefore anyone who commits any of these abominations must be {{karet|cut off}} from among his people.
You must keep My charge not to practice any of the abominable customs that were practiced before you, so that you do not defile yourselves by them. I am the LORD your God.”

ervah.gloss: Nakedness, shame, or exposed vulnerability. The recurring phrase to uncover someone's nakedness is this chapter's euphemism for sexual relations, framing each prohibited union as an exposure of shame that God's law refuses to permit.

zimmah.gloss: Depravity, lewdness, or wicked scheming. A strong term of moral condemnation applied here to marrying both a woman and her close relatives, marking the act not as a minor irregularity but as a serious moral corruption.

toevah.gloss: Abomination, something detestable. Used across the Old Testament for a wide range of practices God finds repugnant, including idolatry and dishonest business dealings, not a single narrow category, though it carries real moral weight wherever it appears.

karet.gloss: To be cut off. A severe covenant penalty, whose precise mechanism, whether divine judgment, execution, or exclusion from the community, is debated, but whose seriousness marks these violations as a fundamental breach of covenant life.

basic.context: This chapter forbids a specific list of sexual relations, incest with close relatives, adultery, child sacrifice to the god Molech, same sex relations, and bestiality, presenting them as the practices of Egypt and Canaan that Israel must not imitate.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter's moral core is treated by the New Testament as enduring, not merely old covenant ceremony; Paul cites a case like this directly in 1 Corinthians 5 and reaffirms several of these categories in Romans 1 and 1 Corinthians 6. The specific civil penalties tied to Israel's land and nationhood, spelled out further in chapter 20, are distinct from that enduring moral core, and Christians today do not enforce them as civil law. This is a chapter that needs to be handled honestly, neither softened nor weaponized.
basic.originalLanguages: The recurring phrase to uncover nakedness, ervah, frames each forbidden union as an exposure of shame. Some acts are called zimmah, depravity, or toevah, abomination, strong moral terms used elsewhere in Scripture for idolatry and injustice as well, showing these are treated as serious moral wrongs, not mere ritual irregularities.
basic.typology: The warning that the land will vomit out the defiled anticipates final judgment on unrepented sin; yet Christ Himself was cut off from the land of the living in His people's place, Isaiah 53:8, so that those who turn to Him escape the ultimate exclusion this chapter warns of.
basic.christ: Paul names sins from exactly this category among the Corinthians and then writes, 'and such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, showing that the gospel neither minimizes this chapter's seriousness nor leaves anyone without hope of full forgiveness and change.
basic.god: God's holiness includes a real, creation rooted design for sexuality that is not culturally relative, and He grieves when that design is violated because real people, and the created order itself, are wounded by it; yet He is also the God who washes, sanctifies, and justifies those who turn to Him, whatever their past.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 5:1 addresses a case resembling verse 8 directly. Romans 1:24-27 echoes this chapter's categories in describing humanity's rebellion against creation's order. Matthew 19:4-6 shows Jesus rooting marriage in Genesis 1 and 2, the same creational foundation this chapter assumes. 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 offers full forgiveness and transformation to those entangled in exactly these sins.
basic.oneStory: God's design for sexuality in creation, one man and one woman in marriage, is guarded here against every distortion, not to shame the human body but to protect what He made good. That same design is honored by Christ, whose gospel judges sin honestly, including sexual sin, while washing, forgiving, and remaking anyone who turns to Him.

context.literary:
Leviticus 18 has a clear frame. It opens and closes with the same concern: do not follow 'the practices of the land of Egypt' or 'of the land of Canaan,' verse 3, and do not practise 'the abominable customs that were practiced before you,' verse 30. The opening and the closing both carry the formula 'I am the LORD your God,' verses 2 and 30, and the phrase 'I am the LORD' sounds six times in all, verses 2, 4, 5, 6, 21 and 30. The laws are bracketed by the identity of the one who gives them.

Inside the frame the chapter moves in three steps. Verses 6 to 18 set the boundaries of the family, working outward from the nearest relations: mother and stepmother, sister and half sister, granddaughter, aunts, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law, and a woman together with her daughter or granddaughter. Each is phrased as 'you must not uncover the nakedness of,' and several add a reason drawn from the relationship itself: 'she is your mother,' 'she is your sister,' 'it would dishonor your father.' Verses 19 to 23 then widen to acts outside the family: relations during menstruation, adultery, the offering of children to Molech, relations between men, and bestiality. Verses 24 to 30 give the sanction, not a list of penalties but the picture of the land itself vomiting out those who defile it.

The placement matters. Chapter 17 dealt with blood and the altar; chapter 18 turns to the household and the body; chapter 19 will widen to the neighbour and the whole of life. Chapter 20 repeats many of these same prohibitions with penalties, so that 18 and 20 form a pair around the central call of chapter 19, 'Be holy, because I, the LORD your God, am holy,' Leviticus 19:2. The instructions are addressed to men as heads of households; only verse 23 names a woman as the one acting.
context.historical:
The chapter was given in the wilderness, between an Egypt Israel had left and a Canaan they had not yet entered, and it names both, verse 3. The first hearers had grown up among Egyptian customs, and Egyptian royal families were known to marry close relatives, including siblings. Canaan's religion and culture would soon surround them on every side.

Molech, verse 21, was associated with the Ammonites; Solomon later built a high place for 'Molech the abomination of the Ammonites,' 1 Kings 11:7. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew speaks of making children 'pass through' the fire. The practice returned in Judah's darkest days: Manasseh 'sacrificed his own son in the fire,' 2 Kings 21:6, and Josiah desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom 'so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech,' 2 Kings 23:10. Placing child sacrifice in a chapter about sexual boundaries shows the chapter's real subject: the family as God's gift, which must not be abused or destroyed.

The early history of Israel's own ancestors would have made the first hearers uneasy. Abraham married his half sister Sarah, Genesis 20:12, which verse 9 forbids. Jacob married two sisters while both lived, which verse 18 forbids. Reuben slept with his father's concubine Bilhah, Genesis 35:22, the offence of verse 8. Judah fathered children by his daughter-in-law Tamar, Genesis 38:15-18, the case of verse 15. Moses' own parents were nephew and aunt, Exodus 6:20, a union verse 12 forbids. The law does not whitewash Israel's past; it sets a new standard for a redeemed people.

The land is spoken of almost as a living thing. It 'has become defiled,' God is 'punishing it for its sin,' and it 'will vomit out its inhabitants,' verse 25. For Israel, holding the land was never unconditional.
context.canonical:
The chapter is taken up many times in the Old Testament. Leviticus 20 attaches penalties to many of the same acts and repeats the threat that the land will vomit Israel out, Leviticus 20:22. Ezekiel 22:10-11 charges Jerusalem with uncovering the nakedness of fathers, violating women during menstrual impurity, and defiling daughters-in-law and sisters, almost a point by point indictment from this chapter. Ezekiel 18:6 lists not defiling a neighbour's wife or approaching a woman during her period among the marks of a righteous man. Amos 2:7 condemns a man and his father having relations with the same girl. The story of 2 Kings 17:7-8 explains the northern exile in the terms of verse 3: Israel 'walked in the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out.'

Verse 5 has its own long history. Ezekiel 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:29 quote it as the life-giving purpose of the law that Israel refused. Paul quotes it twice, Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12, to describe the righteousness that is by the law, which he sets against the righteousness of faith.

In the Gospels John the Baptist rebukes Herod on the basis of verse 16: 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife,' Mark 6:18. Jesus grounds marriage in Genesis 2:24, Matthew 19:4-6, the one-flesh union the family boundaries of this chapter assume.

Paul's letters draw on the chapter directly. The man who 'has his father's wife,' 1 Corinthians 5:1, is the case of verse 8, and Paul's instruction to 'expel the wicked man from among you,' 1 Corinthians 5:13, echoes the chapter's language of being cut off. Romans 1:24-27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9 take up the concern of verse 22, and many scholars trace the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 6:9 to the Greek wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that the redemption from Egypt had consequences for the bedroom and the household. The chapter begins not with a rule but with a name, 'I am the LORD your God,' verse 2. Israel was to be different from its neighbours because it belonged to a different God, and nothing expressed that difference more plainly than how a people ordered its families.

He meant the first hearers to protect the vulnerable. Many of the relations forbidden in verses 6 to 18 are ones in which a man had power over a woman living in his household: a stepmother, a half sister, a granddaughter, a daughter-in-law. The reasons given, 'she is your sister,' 'that would shame your family,' show the law guarding the trust on which family life depends. The Molech law, verse 21, extends that protection to children.

He also meant Israel to take the land seriously. The Canaanites were not being driven out because Israel was more righteous, but because the land could no longer bear their deeds, verse 25, compare Genesis 15:16. The same standard would apply to Israel, verse 28. The gift of the land came with the responsibility to keep it clean.

Above all, verse 5 set the tone: these laws were a way of life, 'the man who does these things will live by them.' The first hearers were meant to receive them as the shape of a flourishing life before God, not as arbitrary restrictions.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is plainly prescriptive for Israel, and most of it is carried into the New Testament as moral instruction. The incest laws are assumed in 1 Corinthians 5:1, adultery is forbidden in Exodus 20:14 and throughout the New Testament, and the prohibition of verse 22 is echoed in Romans 1:26-27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9. Paul's call to 'abstain from sexual immorality' and 'not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God,' 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5, has the same shape as verse 3.

The sanctions belong to Israel's life in the land. The church does not apply the civil penalties of Leviticus 20, and its discipline, as Paul describes it in 1 Corinthians 5:11-13, is exclusion from fellowship aimed at repentance, not death. Verse 19 is a harder case: it sits among moral laws, yet it relates to the purity laws of Leviticus 15:24, and Christians differ on whether it continues.

The patriarchal stories are description, not permission. That Abraham, Jacob or Judah did what this chapter later forbids does not make it acceptable. They show why a clear law was needed.

debates.question: How should Christians read Leviticus 18's sexual prohibitions today, given that chapter 20 attaches civil penalties to them and they sit beside purity laws elsewhere in the Torah?

views.label: Enduring moral instruction
views.case: Many interpreters note that the chapter grounds its laws in the nature of family relationships and in God's own name, not in the sanctuary or in Israel's ethnic identity. The Canaanites are judged for these acts though they never received the law, verses 24 and 25, which implies a standard binding on all nations. The New Testament restates the core prohibitions, 1 Corinthians 5:1, 6:9 and Romans 1:26-27, while it expressly sets aside the food laws, Mark 7:19.

views.label: Moral norms distinct from civil sanctions
views.case: Others agree about the moral core but stress that Israel's penalties in chapter 20 belonged to a nation holding a land in covenant, and do not transfer to the church or to civil law in the same form. The New Testament replaces them with church discipline and the call to repentance, 1 Corinthians 5:13.

debates.bearing: Both views hold the moral norms and differ on how Israel's sanctions apply now. The question of how to distinguish lasting moral law from temporary law is best answered by asking how the New Testament itself treats each command.

debates.question: What does verse 5 mean by 'the man who does these things will live by them'?

views.label: The life of the redeemed within the covenant
views.case: In context, verse 5 is spoken to a people already redeemed, 'I am the LORD your God.' Obedience does not earn the covenant but is the way of flourishing within it, as Deuteronomy 30:15-16 sets 'life and goodness' before Israel. Ezekiel 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:29 read it this way, as a gracious gift Israel spurned.

views.label: A principle of life by law-keeping
views.case: Paul quotes the verse in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12 to describe 'the righteousness that is by the law,' which he contrasts with faith. On this reading the verse states the law's own terms: life for the one who fully does it. Since no sinner does, the verse drives the reader to Christ, who kept the law and bore its curse, Galatians 3:13.

debates.bearing: The readings are not opposites. Leviticus offers life to a redeemed people who walk in God's ways; Paul presses the point that, taken as a way to establish one's own righteousness, the same words condemn. Both lead to Christ, 'the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes,' Romans 10:4.

debates.question: Does the prohibition of verse 19, relations during menstruation, still apply?

views.label: Part of the purity system, now fulfilled
views.case: Leviticus 15:24 treats the same act as a matter of ritual uncleanness lasting seven days. On this view verse 19 is a purity law placed here because it concerns sexual relations, and it passes with the purity system, as the food laws do.

views.label: A moral boundary
views.case: Others note that verse 19 sits among moral prohibitions, that Ezekiel 18:6 and 22:10 list it among the marks of righteousness and wickedness, and that Leviticus 20:18 attaches being cut off to it. They take it as a lasting expression of respect for a wife's body.

debates.bearing: The case shows that Leviticus does not always sort its laws into neat categories. Christians should hold the clearly restated moral laws firmly and be charitable where the New Testament is silent.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 6 names the class of forbidden relations with she'er besaro, literally 'the flesh of his flesh,' rendered 'close relative.' Two different words for flesh are joined, and verses 12 and 13 repeat she'er, with a related form in verse 17. The phrase echoes the one-flesh language of Genesis 2:23-24. The logic is that a close relative is already one's own flesh, so the kinship bond itself rules out a sexual one.

Verses 3 to 5 set two sets of chuqqot, statutes or customs, against each other. Israel must not 'walk in their customs,' chuqqotehem, verse 3, but must 'keep My statutes,' chuqqotai, verse 4. The same word names both. The choice is not between custom and no custom but between two ways of walking, the nations' and the LORD's. Leviticus 20:23 repeats the contrast.

Verse 5 promises that the one who keeps them 'will live by them,' wachay bahem. The preposition be can mean 'in them' or 'by means of them.' Read one way, life is lived within the statutes; read the other, life comes through them. Ezekiel 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:29 quote the line, and Paul's use of it in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12 depends on the second nuance.

Verse 18 forbids taking a wife's sister 'as a rival wife,' litsror, from the root tsarar, to bind or to be hostile. The related noun tsarah is the word for Hannah's 'rival' in 1 Samuel 1:6, and the story of Rachel and Leah shows the misery the law foresaw.

Verse 23 calls bestiality tevel, 'a perversion,' a word used again in Leviticus 20:12 of relations with a daughter-in-law, 'they have acted perversely.' It is usually connected with the idea of mixing or confusing, and marks an act that confounds boundaries God has drawn.

The land 'will vomit out,' from qi, verses 25 and 28, a physical and deliberately ugly verb. The land is portrayed as a body that cannot keep down what poisons it, and Leviticus 20:22 uses the same verb. The verbs in verses 25 and 28 are past in form in the Hebrew, as though the judgment on Canaan were already as good as done.

Finally, verse 21 uses chillel, 'profane,' of the name of God. Offering a child to Molech is not only cruelty to the child; it treats the LORD's holy name as common, as Leviticus 20:3 also says.

typology.type: Israel set apart from Egypt and Canaan, Leviticus 18:3
typology.fulfillment: Israel was to walk differently from both the nation it left and the nation it was entering. The church inherits the calling: Peter addresses believers as 'a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' 1 Peter 2:9, and Paul calls them to holiness 'not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God,' 1 Thessalonians 4:5. The escalation is that holiness is no longer tied to a land's borders but to the Spirit who dwells in believers, whose bodies are temples, 1 Corinthians 6:19. The type falls short because Israel's separation was guarded by law and sanction, while the church's rests on a new heart.

typology.type: The one who does these things will live by them, Leviticus 18:5
typology.fulfillment: The promise of life held out to the obedient found only one man who fully met it. Jesus kept the law without sin and so could offer His life for others. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 3:12 and then at once says, 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The correspondence is that life comes through perfect obedience; the escalation is that Christ's obedience becomes the righteousness of those who believe, Romans 10:4. The type falls short in that the law could promise life but could not give the power to live it, Romans 8:3-4.

typology.type: The land vomiting out a defiled people, Leviticus 18:25-28
typology.fulfillment: The land expelled the Canaanites and later Israel itself, 2 Kings 17:7-8. It foreshadows the final judgment, when 'nothing unclean will ever enter' the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:27, and the sexually immoral remain outside, Revelation 22:15. The escalation in Christ is that He Himself was 'cut off from the land of the living' and 'stricken for the transgression of My people,' Isaiah 53:8, taking the exclusion so that sinners may enter. The type falls short because the land's judgment could only expel, while Christ's cross cleanses and brings in.

typology.type: Uncovering nakedness and the covering of shame
typology.fulfillment: From Genesis 3:7 onward nakedness signals shame, and Ham's seeing his father's nakedness, Genesis 9:22, is linked to Canaan, the very land this chapter names. Leviticus 18 forbids exposing the nakedness of another. At the cross Jesus was stripped, and the soldiers divided His garments, John 19:23-24; He 'endured the cross, scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2. The escalation is that the one who never exposed another took exposure on Himself, so that those who put Him on are clothed, Galatians 3:27. The type falls short because the law could forbid shame but not remove it.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through His own words and those of His forerunner. When asked about marriage, Jesus goes behind Moses to 'the beginning,' where the Creator 'made them male and female' and the two become one flesh, Matthew 19:4-6. The family boundaries of Leviticus 18 protect exactly that union. John the Baptist lost his life for applying verse 16 to Herod, Mark 6:18. Jesus also deepened the chapter's demand: adultery begins with the lustful look, Matthew 5:27-28. He does not lower the bar the chapter sets; He raises it to the heart.

It leads to Christ through His genealogy. Matthew names Tamar, 'Judah was the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar,' Matthew 1:3, recalling the union verse 15 forbids. The Messiah's own line runs through the kind of family failure this chapter addresses, and Matthew does not hide it. The Son of God entered a history marked by sexual sin in order to redeem it.

It leads to Christ through His dealings with sinners. At the well in Samaria Jesus named the woman's history plainly, 'you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband,' John 4:18, and then offered her living water. He neither ignored the law nor used it to crush her.

It leads to Christ through verse 5. The promise of life to the one who keeps the statutes is fulfilled in the only man who kept them wholly. Paul places Leviticus 18:5 beside Christ's cross: the law says 'the man who does these things will live by them,' and Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:12-13.

Finally, it leads to Christ through the union the chapter protects. Paul says the one-flesh union of Genesis 2:24 is a 'profound' mystery that speaks of 'Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:31-32. The purity of human marriage points to a greater marriage, 'the marriage of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:7. Sexual faithfulness is a living picture of Christ's faithfulness to His bride, which is part of why its violation is so serious.

The chapter should never be read as though Christ's grace makes its standards irrelevant, nor as though its standards leave no room for grace. Paul holds both in one sentence: 'And that is what some of you were. But you were washed,' 1 Corinthians 6:11.
study.god:
The chapter reveals God first as the Lord of the whole of life. Before any command He gives His name, 'I am the LORD your God,' verse 2, and He repeats it throughout. The ordering of family and sexual life is not a separate, private sphere; it falls under the authority of the God who redeemed Israel. His claim reaches into the most intimate parts of human life.

It shows that God is the protector of the weak. Many of the relations forbidden are ones where a man could exploit a woman under his roof, and verse 21 shields children from being offered to Molech. The chapter's concern for 'your sister,' 'your granddaughter,' 'your daughter-in-law' reflects a God who notices those with little power.

It shows that God is impartial in judgment. He judges the Canaanites for these practices, though they did not have the law at Sinai, and He tells Israel that the land will treat them no differently, verse 28. There is no favouritism in God's holiness. Genesis 15:16 had already shown Him waiting patiently until 'the iniquity of the Amorites' was complete; His judgment is neither hasty nor arbitrary.

It shows that God's holiness touches creation itself. The land is defiled, punished and made to vomit, verse 25. Human sin is not only interpersonal; it damages the world God made and entrusted to people. That is the logic behind Paul's statement that the whole creation groans, Romans 8:22.

It shows that God's name can be profaned, verse 21. What human beings do with their bodies and their children reflects on the God they claim to serve. Holiness in life is a way of honouring His name before the watching nations.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to present their bodies to God, 1 Corinthians 6:20, 'you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body,' and to trust that the God who draws boundaries does so as the author of life. His commands in verse 5 are the path of life, not its enemy.

crossReferences.note: The man calls the woman 'bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,' and the two become one flesh. Leviticus 18:6 uses kinship language of flesh for close relatives, so that the family bond itself excludes the one-flesh bond with anyone already of one's own flesh.

Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness. The phrase is the chapter's own idiom, and the connection with Canaan explains why Leviticus 18:3 names the land of Canaan as the source of the practices Israel must not follow.

God tells Abram that the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete. Leviticus 18:24-28 describes that iniquity now complete and the land vomiting out its inhabitants, showing that the conquest was judgment long delayed, not favouritism.

Ezekiel charges Jerusalem with uncovering fathers' nakedness, violating women in their impurity, and defiling a daughter-in-law and a sister, almost a list drawn from Leviticus 18. The people who were to be different had become like Canaan, and exile followed.

Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5 to describe the righteousness that is by the law and contrasts it with the righteousness of faith. His point is that life through the law requires doing, while the gospel announces Christ as the end of the law for all who believe.

Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5 again and then says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse. The law's promise of life to the obedient is fulfilled by the obedient One who bears the curse for the disobedient.

John the Baptist tells Herod that it is not lawful to have his brother's wife, applying Leviticus 18:16 directly to a king. It shows the chapter was still held as binding in Jesus' day, and that John was willing to die for it.

A man in the church has his father's wife, the offence of Leviticus 18:8, and Paul calls it intolerable even among pagans. He rebukes the church for pride and calls for grief and discipline, applying the chapter's seriousness within the new covenant community.

Paul lists those who will not inherit the kingdom, including the sexually immoral and adulterers and men who perform homosexual acts, then declares that some of the Corinthians had been such but were washed, sanctified and justified. The chapter's standards and Christ's cleansing stand together.

Paul tells Gentile believers that God's will is their holiness, abstaining from sexual immorality and not living in lustful passion like the Gentiles. The contrast with those who do not know God is the same contrast Leviticus 18:3 draws with Egypt and Canaan.

Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says the one-flesh union is a profound mystery about Christ and the church. The boundaries Leviticus 18 draws around marriage protect a union that is meant to picture the faithfulness of Christ to His people.

study.oneStory:
At creation God made humanity male and female and joined the man and the woman as one flesh, naked and unashamed, Genesis 2:24-25. The fall turned nakedness into shame, Genesis 3:7, and very soon the story links the uncovering of nakedness with Canaan, Genesis 9:22. Leviticus 18 answers what the fall had broken in the family: God draws boundaries around marriage and kinship so that the household can again be a place of trust rather than exploitation.

The chapter also answers the promise to Abraham. God had said He would give the land to Abraham's descendants when the iniquity of its people was complete, Genesis 15:16. Here that moment arrives. The land will expel its inhabitants, and Israel will receive it, but on the same terms of holiness.

It sets up much of what follows in Israel's story. The history books show Israel walking in the customs of the nations, 2 Kings 17:7-8; kings offer their children in the fire, 2 Kings 21:6; and the prophets indict Jerusalem with this chapter's own words, Ezekiel 22:10-11. The land vomits Israel out as it did the Canaanites, and during the exile the land rests, Leviticus 26:34. The law showed the way of life but could not produce a people who walked in it.

The story turns in Christ, who keeps the law that promises life, bears the curse of those who broke it, and forms a new people who are washed, sanctified and justified, 1 Corinthians 6:11. The church is called to holiness in the body as a temple of the Spirit.

The new creation brings the story to its end in a wedding. John hears the cry, 'the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready,' Revelation 19:7. The one-flesh union of Eden, guarded in Leviticus 18, was always a sign of this greater union. In the city nothing unclean will enter, Revelation 21:27, and the shame that began in the garden will be gone for good.

quiz.q: What reason does God give for these commands in verses 1-5?

options.text: He is the LORD their God who is bringing them out of Egypt and into Canaan, and they must not follow either land's customs.
options.note: Verses 2-4 give this reasoning, anchored in God's own identity as the LORD.

options.text: Because the surrounding nations were militarily weaker than Israel.
options.note: This is not the stated reason; the text grounds the commands in covenant relationship with the LORD, not military comparison.

options.text: No reason at all is given for these commands.
options.note: Verses 1-5 explicitly state the reasoning, repeated as 'I am the LORD.'

options.text: Because Moses personally disliked these practices.
options.note: The text attributes these commands to the LORD speaking to Moses, not to Moses' personal preference.

quiz.q: What phrase is repeated throughout this chapter to anchor its commands?

options.text: "I am the LORD," tying every command back to God's own identity and authority.
options.note: This phrase recurs at verses 2, 4, 5, 6, 21, and 30.

options.text: "As your ancestors commanded."
options.note: The text grounds these laws in God's own word, not ancestral tradition.

options.text: "For the sake of Egypt's approval."
options.note: The chapter explicitly rejects Egypt's customs rather than seeking its approval.

options.text: No repeated phrase occurs in the chapter.
options.note: "I am the LORD" recurs multiple times through the chapter.

quiz.q: According to verse 21, what specific practice involving children is forbidden here?

options.text: Giving one's children to be sacrificed to Molech.
options.note: Verse 21 names this practice explicitly and calls it a profaning of God's name.

options.text: Sending children to be educated in Egypt.
options.note: The verse specifically addresses child sacrifice to Molech, not education.

options.text: Selling children into indentured labor.
options.note: That subject is addressed elsewhere in the law; verse 21 specifically concerns sacrifice to Molech.

options.text: No mention of children occurs in this chapter.
options.note: Verse 21 explicitly addresses this practice.

quiz.q: What warning does God give about the land itself in verses 24-28?

options.text: The land will vomit out its inhabitants if they defile it, just as it did the nations before them.
options.note: Verses 25 and 28 state this warning directly.

options.text: The land would become more fertile the more these practices continued.
options.note: The text states the opposite: the land becomes defiled and expels those who defile it.

options.text: The land's fate has no connection to Israel's conduct.
options.note: Verses 24-28 explicitly connect the land's fate to the conduct of its inhabitants.

options.text: No warning about the land is given.
options.note: Verses 25 and 28 explicitly warn about the land.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament handle the reality of sexual sin this chapter addresses?

options.text: It names such sin honestly while declaring that those entangled in it can be washed, sanctified, and justified in Christ.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 does exactly this.

options.text: It avoids the subject entirely.
options.note: Paul addresses these categories directly in Romans 1, 1 Corinthians 5, and 1 Corinthians 6.

options.text: It treats such sin as permanently unforgivable.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 6:11 explicitly offers forgiveness, washing, and a new identity in Christ.

options.text: There is no New Testament connection to this subject.
options.note: Multiple New Testament passages engage this chapter's concerns directly.

questions: This chapter grounds sexual ethics not in cultural convention but in the character of the LORD Himself. Where do you unconsciously let surrounding culture, rather than Scripture, set your convictions on matters of sex, marriage, or identity?

God warns that certain practices defile not only the sinner but even the land itself. How seriously do you take the idea that sin has effects reaching beyond yourself, into your family, community, or church?

Paul tells the Corinthians, some of whom had lived in exactly the sins this chapter names, that they were washed, sanctified, and justified. Is there shame from your own past, sexual or otherwise, that you have not yet let the gospel actually reach?

This chapter calls Israel to be different from both the culture they came from and the culture they were entering. Where is God calling you to a costly difference from the culture around you right now?
How can you hold together, without flinching from either side, the honesty of this chapter about sin's seriousness and the mercy of Christ toward anyone who turns to Him?

translationNotes.note: Close relative renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning near of flesh, sharing the same root sense that runs through the following list's repeated formula of uncovering nakedness.

Molech was a deity associated with child sacrifice in the ancient Near East; some scholars debate whether every instance in the Old Testament refers to literal immolation or, in some contexts, dedication, but Leviticus 20:2-5 makes clear this practice incurred the death penalty as a capital offense.

The phrase rendered abomination, toevah, is used across the Old Testament for a range of practices, including idolatry and dishonest business dealings, and always carries strong moral disapproval rather than mere ritual irregularity.
